slides.text: Welcome to practicals twenty seven and twenty eight: P C A in Python, with the wine quality and breast cancer datasets.

Practical twenty seven implements P C A: load and scale, check V I F, fit P C A, variance explained, and how many P Cs. Practical twenty eight visualises and interprets: loadings heat map, P C scatter, loading plot, and a worked breast cancer example. We use wine quality, six thousand four hundred ninety seven rows, as the main example, and breast cancer, five sixty nine rows and thirty features, as the worked example.

Step one: load the data, take the eleven lab measurements as features, and scale with Standard Scaler. P C A follows the largest variance. Total sulfur dioxide has a standard deviation of fifty six point five, density only point oh oh three. Without scaling, P C one would explain ninety five percent only because sulfur dioxide has the biggest numbers. After scaling every feature has standard deviation one.

Step two: check multicollinearity with V I F. It is the diagonal of the inverse correlation matrix, the same result as running eleven separate regressions. Density has fifteen point nine one, above ten, so serious. Residual sugar is seven point two three. Drop density and the largest V I F is two point eight four. P C A components always have V I F of one.

Step three: fit P C A, keeping all eleven components, and call fit transform to learn the axes and give each wine its P C values. The result is still six thousand four hundred ninety seven by eleven, because P C A only rotates the axes. The correlation between P Cs is zero, so there is no repeated information.

Step four: variance explained. Eigenvalue is the variance carried by a P C; on scaled data the total is eleven, one per feature. P C one has eigenvalue three point oh three, twenty seven point five percent. P C two is twenty two point seven. Together they hold fifty percent, and seven P Cs reach ninety percent.
Plot the scree plot, one bar per P C, which shows an elbow after P C three, and the cumulative plot, which crosses the ninety percent line at seven components.

Step five: how many components to keep? Eigenvalue above one gives three. Passing a number below one, like zero point nine, to n components means keep enough P Cs for ninety percent of the variance, giving seven. The elbow gives three for a quick look, Kaiser three for scaled data, and a ninety percent target seven to keep most information.

Step six: loadings show what each P C is made of. Draw them as a heat map. P C one is white style, sulfur dioxide and sugar, against red style, volatile acidity and chlorides. P C two is heavy, density, against light, alcohol. P C three is acidity, citric and fixed, against pH.

Step seven: plot each wine on P C one and P C two, coloured by type. The average position of red wines is minus two point five one on P C one, white wines plus point eight two. P C A never saw type, yet red and white separate along P C one, so the name red versus white style is right.

Step eight: the loading plot shows how the features point. One quiver call draws one arrow per feature, all in one command. Same direction means features rise together, like the two sulfur dioxides. Opposite means one up, one down, like density and alcohol.

The same code on the breast cancer data. The largest V I F is mean radius at three thousand eight hundred six. P C one and P C two explain forty four point three and nineteen percent. Seven of thirty P Cs reach ninety percent, and six have eigenvalue above one. Thirty features become two numbers that separate benign from malignant, with P C one meaning large, irregular shape, on the malignant side.

What the lab showed. Scale, P C A, fit transform: three lines of code. Wine: P C one plus P C two is fifty percent; three P Cs by Kaiser, seven for ninety percent. Loadings name the P Cs, and the P C scatter confirms the names. And on breast cancer, thirty features become two P Cs that separate the diagnoses. Thanks for watching.
